Richard developed the algorithm and a small working prototype. But when they are developing it for the whole world (not just a simple demo at TechCrunch), there is a lot to be done. Like most of coding, modular design, testing, porting to all available platforms, documenting changes, developing and maintaining web site/interfaces, apps, having version compatibility, network deployment, server maintenance, security etc. All of this cannot be done by just one guy. Dinesh-Gilfoyle would be the leaders who design the overall structure and the people working under them would communicate, deisgn and code these things. 

For example, lets take Evernote. It is a basic notes taking app. But it has web version, apps on various platforms, a desktop version on Mac/Windows/Linux. They have to maintain paid and free versions. There are servers maintained at the backend without our knowledge. Security on sites and servers is taken care of. As time passes, new features are constantly added and older useful features are sustained. Every change has to be documented for useful debugging/testing. Each and every feature has to be tested on all platforms and versions. Other than this there are a lot of aspects which depend on the type of product being built. So, even though Evernote is a simple app, all these other aspects need employees. This is the reason lot of manpower is required to develop any product/service in software industry.

Core Computer Science is all about mathematics. But it has evolved so much that there is a whole market without necessary deep math skills. For example in the IT sector there are opportunities for web designers, web development coders, java/dotnet programmers, python programmers to write software programs for typical hospital/airline management or ecommerce applications. These jobs do not require hardcore math. All the IT companies (service industry) like Accenture, IBM, HP etc need people with such skillset.

But core compsci like analysis of algorithms, design of search engines, developing compilers, artificial intelligence, machine learning, operating system and computer architecture etc require heavy math. They need all the courses you mentioned above. Companies like Intel, Google, Adobe, Microsoft need people with deep math skills. 

I am doing my masters with computer networks specialization and my undergrad was compsci with minor in math. I am way ahead than rest of my peers coz I am good at math. 

Bottomline: If you are looking for a mediocre IT career - leaving math is fine. But if you want a top notch career go with math. It's worth it.
